blocks.text: Token classification loss assigns a separate label to every individual token in a sequence, rather than one single label for the whole sequence, computing cross-entropy loss at each token position independently, the loss structure behind tasks like named entity recognition and part-of-speech tagging.

This topic distinguishes token classification loss from the sequence level and generation focused losses covered earlier in this module, closing out the core loss function landscape before this course moves into optimizers and training infrastructure.
1. What Token Classification Means

blocks.alt: One label for a whole sequence is compared against one label per token

blocks.text: Where a traditional classification task, covered in the earlier Cross-Entropy Loss topic, assigns one label to an entire input, token classification assigns a separate label to every individual token, such as tagging each word in a sentence as a person name, a location, or neither.
2. A Separate Label Per Token, Not Per Sequence

blocks.alt: Token one gets label A, token two gets label B, token three gets label A again

blocks.text: This means the training data for a token classification task pairs every single token with its own individual correct label, rather than one label describing the input as a whole, a meaningfully different data shape from the instruction datasets covered in the Dataset Preparation module.
3. Cross-Entropy Applied Per Token

blocks.alt: Each token position gets its own cross-entropy calculation, then the results get averaged

blocks.text: The actual loss computation applies cross-entropy independently at every token position, exactly the same underlying mechanism covered in the Cross-Entropy Loss topic, just computed once per token rather than once per sequence, then averaged together to get one overall loss value.

code.content:
# A simplified token classification loss
predictions = model(input_tokens)  # one prediction per token position
loss = cross_entropy(predictions, token_labels)
average_loss = loss.mean()

blocks.text: 4. Common Token Classification Tasks

blocks.alt: Named entity recognition and part-of-speech tagging are common token classification tasks

blocks.text: Named entity recognition, identifying which words refer to people, organizations, or locations, and part-of-speech tagging, labeling each word grammatical role, are two of the most common token classification tasks, both requiring exactly this per token labeling structure.

blocks.text: 5. Handling Subword Tokenization Mismatches

blocks.alt: One word can split into multiple subword tokens, requiring label alignment

blocks.text: Since tokenization, covered in the Tokenization Pipeline topic, often splits one real word into several subword tokens, token classification labels, usually assigned per real word, need to be carefully aligned to the resulting subword tokens, typically by applying the same label to every subword piece of a given word or only computing loss on the first subword piece.

blocks.title: This alignment step is easy to overlook
blocks.content: A mismatch between word level labels and subword level tokens is a common, subtle bug in token classification pipelines, worth checking explicitly rather than assuming tokenization and labeling automatically stay in sync.

blocks.text: 6. Class Imbalance in Token Classification

blocks.alt: Many common class tokens are compared against few rare class tokens, creating imbalance

blocks.text: Token classification tasks often have a heavily imbalanced label distribution, most tokens in a typical sentence are not a named entity at all, while entity labels themselves are comparatively rare, a class imbalance worth accounting for, sometimes through weighted loss, when the rare classes are actually the ones that matter most for the task.
7. Token Classification vs Sequence Classification Loss

Token classification loss and the sequence level classification covered through cross-entropy earlier in this module solve related but distinct problems, one label per token versus one label for an entire input, and choosing the right one depends entirely on whether the task genuinely needs per token granularity or a single overall judgment.
8. Masking Special Tokens During Loss Computation

blocks.alt: Special tokens are excluded from the loss calculation

blocks.text: Special tokens, covered in the Tokenization Pipeline topic, padding tokens, sequence start and end markers, do not carry real classification labels and are excluded from the loss calculation, similar in spirit to the label masking used for supervised fine-tuning covered in the Causal Language Modeling Loss topic.
9. Evaluating Token Classification Models

Token classification models are typically evaluated using per token or per entity precision, recall, and related metrics rather than raw loss alone, since a task like named entity recognition cares specifically about correctly identifying complete entity spans, a nuance raw loss does not directly capture.
Worked Example

A team fine-tuning a model for named entity recognition in legal documents builds a token classification dataset where every token is labeled as either part of a party name, a date, a monetary amount, or none of the above, and discovers early on that the none category vastly outnumbers the others.

They apply class weighting to their cross-entropy loss calculation, giving the rarer entity categories more relative weight, and observe meaningfully improved recall on those rare categories after retraining, addressing the class imbalance that a naive unweighted loss had been quietly under-emphasizing.
Common Mistakes

items: Mismatching word level labels against subword tokens without a clear alignment strategy
Ignoring class imbalance in a token classification task where the rare classes matter most
Including special tokens like padding in the loss calculation instead of masking them out
Evaluating a token classification model using loss alone, without task specific metrics like entity level precision and recall

blocks.text: Practice

For a short sentence, sketch what a token by token named entity label sequence would look like, then consider how you would handle a case where one entity name splits across two subword tokens during tokenization.
Key Takeaway

Token classification loss applies cross-entropy independently at every token position rather than once per sequence, powering tasks like named entity recognition and part-of-speech tagging, and doing it well requires carefully aligning labels to subword tokens, accounting for class imbalance, and masking special tokens out of the loss calculation.
